transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Brewer (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Lyra Head of ML), Priya Desai (Lyra Platform Eng), Marcus Lee (Lyra SRE)

Summary (auto): POC scoping focused on benchmark planning and harness integration. Discussed workload sizing, streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs, cold vs warm KV cache, target latency/throughput, security/access for running benchmarks, and next steps to share harness and schedule runs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Brewer: hey everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:02] Jordan Kim: yeah, loud and clear, thanks Alex.
[00:05] Sofia Martinez: great, i'll do a quick agenda — benchmark harness integration, what Lyra's scripts look like, streaming vs non-streaming, success criteria and timelines. then we'll map owners.
[00:15] Priya Desai: quick context — we run inference for summarization and entity extraction across our analytics pipeline. typical input lengths 256-1024 tokens, about 20k requests per day, peak concurrency around 120 concurrent sessions, sometimes bursty.
[00:30] Marcus Lee: from infra side we care about VPC-only access, KMS for keys, and that we can audit runs. SOC2 is table stakes.
[00:40] Alex Brewer: understood. for the POC we usually run two phases — functional correctness + quality, then throughput/latency benchmarks. for the harness we can either run your scripts inside our harness or run our harness pointing at your endpoint, do you have preference?
[00:55] Jordan Kim: preference is to run our scripts — they exercise our tokenization and pre/post-processing. but we can adapt. main ask is we need reproducible numbers so both approaches should be possible.
[01:10] Sofia Martinez: cool. we typically accept customer-provided scripts as dockerized workloads or a small shim. recommend shard of 100k tokens for perf, but you asked for 1M tokens earlier, that's fine. we will provide example wrappers.
[01:30] Priya Desai: our scripts currently assume streaming responses for progressive display; we also have non-streaming batch jobs. curious on the perf delta.
[01:45] Sofia Martinez: streaming vs non-streaming — two different bottlenecks. streaming adds more latency per token but reduces tail latency for first token, and often needs different concurrency handling on the server. We can instrument both. typical numbers — non-streaming throughput (tokens/sec) will be higher, but streaming gives better perceived latency.
[02:05] Alex Brewer: can you share a target SLO? e.g., 95th perc latency under X ms for streaming first token, and overall tokens/sec for batching.
[02:18] Jordan Kim: 95p for first token < 300ms for interactive flows, end-to-end summarization < 2s for typical 512 tokens. throughput target for batch nightly jobs is 50k tokens/sec across the cluster.
[02:35] Marcus Lee: and cost target — we'd like to understand per-token cost and also the Dedicated pricing if we move there.
[02:45] Sofia Martinez: we'll run both hosted and a sample Dedicated-like run with reserved capacity emulation so you can see unit economics. the harness will collect token counts, latency percentiles, GPU utilization, and KV cache hit rates.
[03:05] Priya Desai: about KV cache — we have a lot of repeated prefixes, can Redwood do prefix caching?
[03:12] Sofia Martinez: yes, prefix/KV caching supported. important for summarization because prompts are often similar. in the harness we'll run cold vs warm cache tests to show delta — warm cache can improve tokens/sec by 20-50% depending on workload.
[03:30] Jordan Kim: good. for the harness inputs, what format do you need? we have jsonl with prompt, metadata, and expected tokens.
[03:38] Alex Brewer: jsonl is ideal. we'll need an example of tokenization used — GPT-style or byte-pair? if your tokenization differs we need to normalize
[03:50] Priya Desai: we use tiktoken-like BPE, will include tokenizer version.
[03:55] Sofia Martinez: perfect. on the orchestration side we have a benchmark runner that supports two modes: streaming (websocket/chunked-HTTP) and non-streaming (batch HTTP). we'll provide runbooks for both.
[04:08] Marcus Lee: network/setup questions — we need to keep data in our VPC, can we run the harness from our VPC and point to Redwood Private?
[04:18] Alex Brewer: yes, for Private deployment we can run the harness inside your VPC, or you can run our harness that tunnels to your test endpoint. we'll need temporary credentials for the test deployment.
[04:30] Jordan Kim: can you run a few sample runs to show what telemetry looks like?
[04:36] Sofia Martinez: yes, we'll share a sample run dashboard — token-level breakdown, latency p95/p99, GPU occupancy, and error rates.
[04:45] Alex Brewer: on measurement, recommended metrics: tokens_per_sec, requests_per_sec, latency_p50/p95/p99 first_token and last_token, GPU_util, batch_size distribution, kv_cache_hit_rate, and cost_per_1M_tokens.
[05:05] Priya Desai: do you simulate noisy neighbor or contention?
[05:10] Sofia Martinez: we can schedule synthetic contention by launching background workers or by resizing the instance pool; we'll show both steady-state and burst scenarios.
[05:22] Jordan Kim: timeline? we'd like results in two weeks ideally.
[05:25] Alex Brewer: realistic timeline: share harness & scripts by Jan 3, quick initial runs in first week (warm-up, smoke), full benchmark run scheduled in week of Jan 4-10, results + analysis by Jan 12. feels tight but doable.
[05:40] Marcus Lee: security docs — will you provide SOC2 report and specifics for how logs are stored during the run?
[05:48] Alex Brewer: yes, we'll attach SOC2 and the redaction/audit plan. for the POC run we'll support ephemeral logging and we can disable retention upon request.
[05:58] Priya Desai: for our internal stake holders, we also want a reproducible script to re-run the benchmarks.
[06:05] Sofia Martinez: harness will be a repo with dockerized runner + README + example configs (qps, concurrency levels, token_limit, streaming bool). you'll be able to change concurrency and sequence length matrix.
[06:18] Jordan Kim: curious about quantization — do you test int8 or float16?
[06:24] Sofia Martinez: we test float16 and int8 QAT profiles where applicable; we will surface accuracy vs perf delta. for some models int8 gives 1.2-1.5x perf boost with small quality delta. we will run sensitivity tests.
[06:40] Alex Brewer: another practical — please include a matrix of model variants and expected kernel choices; we might want to compare open models you host vs our in-house tuned model.
[06:50] Priya Desai: regarding streaming specifically, we rely on chunked responses to render live progress. how do you measure first-byte latency vs per-chunk latency?
[06:58] Sofia Martinez: harness measures first_byte_time separately and then chunk_inter_arrival times; we report distribution of chunk sizes and inter-arrival times.
[07:10] Jordan Kim: good. also we sometimes do long sequences (~2k tokens) for report generation; will the harness support extended context runs?
[07:18] Sofia Martinez: yes, we'll include a sequence length sweep up to 4096 tokens to capture memory/latency behavior. we'll note whether we hit kv cache eviction or memory pressure.
[07:30] Marcus Lee: on cost, please show both per-token cost and per-request cost for different batching settings.
[07:36] Alex Brewer: we'll produce cost simulations using your QPS and our observed tokens/sec and GPU hours.
[07:44] Priya Desai: what about failure modes — timeouts, partial streams, retried chunks?
[07:50] Sofia Martinez: harness records error types, retries, and also does chaos scenarios if you want — e.g., mid-stream drop, packet loss emulation. we can run a limited chaos pass.
[08:02] Jordan Kim: ok, that helps. for acceptance criteria — what should we set?
[08:06] Alex Brewer: propose acceptance items: 1) functional parity (outputs meet quality bar on a small eval set), 2) latency SLOs met for streaming/non-streaming (95p first_token < 300ms interactive), 3) throughput target for batch within 10% of target (50k tokens/sec), 4) security checks passed (VPC/KMS/audit).
[08:26] Jordan Kim: sounds good, add cost threshold — cost_per_1M_tokens under $X (we'll define X after initial run).
[08:34] Priya Desai: add reproducibility — benchmarks must be re-runnable with same configs.
[08:40] Alex Brewer: noted. we'll include a reproducibility checklist.
[08:48] Marcus Lee: any blocking items from our side?
[08:50] Priya Desai: need to ensure we can share sanitized sample data and our tokenizer. also need temporary peering and test KMS keys.
[08:58] Alex Brewer: good. we'll send a pre-run checklist.
[09:03] Sofia Martinez: ok, i'll capture concrete run matrix: concurrency levels [10,50,120], sequence lengths [256,512,1024,2048], streaming on/off, cache cold/warm, model variants [open-1, open-2, rw-quant-int8], and quant profiles. we'll attach this to the harness README.
[09:25] Jordan Kim: one more — do you support client-side backpressure / batching guidance?
[09:30] Sofia Martinez: yes we'll include recommended client-side batching heuristics and suggested queue sizes for low-latency interactive flows.
[09:36] Alex Brewer: ok moving to wrap-up. recap of next steps: Alex send harness + README, Priya share sample inputs and tokenizer, Marcus open VPC/KMS access, Sofia prepare streaming vs non-streaming notes and run matrix.
[09:52] Jordan Kim: timeline agrees. thanks everyone.
[09:55] Alex Brewer: thanks, we'll follow up over email and create calendar invites for the benchmark run.
[09:58] End of call.
